n: Answering the people’s fear (17:12-13), the Lord speaks directly to Aaron. The priests will carry responsibility for any offense against the sanctuary, shielding the people.

f.w: bear the iniquity of the sanctuary
f.g: Take responsibility for any wrongdoing connected with the holy place and its service.

n: The rest of the tribe of Levi will assist Aaron, but only Aaron and his sons serve before the ark itself. The word “joined” plays on the name Levi, which sounds like the Hebrew for “joined.”
Levites guard and care for the tabernacle, but they must not touch the holy vessels or the altar. Boundaries protect both the Levites and the priests.

f.g: nigh = near
Duty, assigned responsibility.

n: The Levites will handle all the tabernacle work, and no unauthorized person may come near.

f.g: Here, anyone not appointed to that service.

n: If the priests faithfully guard the sanctuary and altar, God’s wrath will no longer break out on Israel as it did with Korah.
God calls the Levites a gift — given to the priests to help with the work of the tabernacle. Service in God’s house is a privilege, not a burden.
The priesthood itself is called “a service of gift” — something God gives, not something a person can seize. Only priests may serve at the altar and inside the veil.

f.g: Behind the curtain separating the holy place from the most holy place.

n: Now the Lord explains how priests will be supported: they receive portions of the offerings Israel brings. “Anointing” refers to their being set apart for this work.

f.g: Because they were anointed (consecrated) as priests.
Portions set apart or “lifted up” for the Lord and given to His priests.

n: The “most holy” portions — parts of the grain, sin, and guilt offerings not burned on the altar — belong to the priests.

f.g: oblation = offering
An offering for guilt, often involving repayment for wrong done (Leviticus 5-6).

n: These most holy portions must be eaten in a holy place, and only by the males of the priestly family.

f.g: Likely the sacred tabernacle court area, rather than the inner room itself.

n: Other offerings could be shared with the priest’s whole family, sons and daughters alike, as long as they were ritually clean.

f.g: Portions waved before the Lord as a sign of presenting them to Him.
Ritually pure, not under any temporary impurity.

n: The best of the oil, wine, and grain — the first part of each harvest — also goes to the priests.
Whatever first ripens in the land and is brought to the Lord becomes the priests’ food.
Anything permanently dedicated to the Lord belongs to the priests.

f.g: Hebrew ḥerem — something wholly and irrevocably given to God.

n: Every firstborn belongs to the Lord. Firstborn sons and firstborn of unclean animals (like donkeys) were to be “redeemed” — bought back — instead of sacrificed.

f.g: Opens the womb — that is, is firstborn.

n: A firstborn son was redeemed at one month old for five shekels of silver, a fixed price measured by the sanctuary’s standard weight.

f.g: A gerah was the smallest weight unit; twenty made one shekel.

n: Firstborn calves, lambs, and kids, however, are not redeemed. They are holy and are sacrificed on the altar.

f.g: firstling = firstborn animal

n: The meat from these firstborn sacrifices goes to the priests, like the breast and right shoulder of the peace offerings.
God seals this arrangement as “a covenant of salt” — salt preserves and does not decay, so the phrase means a lasting, unbreakable covenant.
A beautiful promise: Aaron will own no land in Canaan, because the Lord Himself is his portion and inheritance. Those who serve God are cared for by Him.

f.w: I am thy part and thine inheritance

n: The Levites receive Israel’s tithes — a tenth of the harvest — as their inheritance in return for their tabernacle service.
Ordinary Israelites must not approach the tabernacle in ways reserved for its ministers, so that no one bears sin and dies.
The Levites take on that sacred work and its responsibilities. Because of this calling, they receive no tribal land.
Instead of land, the tithes offered to the Lord are given to the Levites as their inheritance.

f.g: A tithe is a tenth part, given to God.

n: Now the Lord gives Moses a message for the Levites themselves.
The Levites must also pay tithing: a tenth of the tithes they receive is offered to the Lord. No one is exempt from giving.

f.w: a tenth part of the tithe
f.g: Often called “the tithe of the tithe.”

n: God counts the Levites’ tithe as if it were their own harvest from field and winepress. Their offering is just as acceptable as a farmer’s.

f.g: reckoned = counted, credited
In KJV English “corn” means grain, such as wheat or barley.

n: The Levites’ tithe goes to Aaron the priest.
They must give from the best portion, not the leftovers. Giving God the best is a sign of real devotion.
Once they have given the best part, the rest is theirs to use like any farmer’s harvest.
Levites and their families may eat it anywhere. It is their honest wages for serving at the tabernacle.
If they give the best portion as commanded, they will be blameless. But to treat holy gifts carelessly would profane them — a warning to handle sacred things with respect.

f.g: Profane, treat as common something that is holy.
